title: Hyde Park & Kensington Gardens
intro: From the Royal Albert Hall through Kensington Gardens to Hyde Park Corner: Peter Pan, the Serpentine and a palace. Also look out for Albert Gate on Knightsbridge, whose two stags came from the old Ranger's Lodge in Green Park, and Marble Arch at the park's north-east corner, moved here from Buckingham Palace in 1851.

stops.name: Royal Albert Hall
stops.note: Start on the steps. Queen Victoria named it after Albert when she laid the foundation stone in 1867.

stops.name: Albert Memorial
stops.note: Albert holds the catalogue of his 1851 Great Exhibition.

stops.name: Round Pond & Kensington Palace
stops.note: Swans and geese, with Diana's old home across the water.

stops.name: Diana Memorial Playground
stops.note: A pirate ship inspired by Peter Pan. The family stop.

stops.name: Peter Pan Statue
stops.note: J.M. Barrie had it put up secretly overnight in 1912, so children would think it had appeared by magic.

stops.name: Italian Gardens
stops.note: Fountains said to be Albert's gift to Victoria.

stops.name: Serpentine Bridge & Lake
stops.note: Where Kensington Gardens becomes Hyde Park. Every Christmas morning swimmers race here for the Peter Pan Cup.

stops.name: Diana Memorial Fountain
stops.note: Opened by the Queen in 2004. You can dip your feet in.

stops.name: Rotten Row
stops.note: Thought to come from 'Route du Roi', the King's Road. Lit with oil lamps in 1690, often called the first lit road in England.

stops.name: Achilles statue
stops.note: Not really Achilles. It's London's tribute to Wellington, cast from French cannon captured in his victories and paid for by the women of England. When it was unveiled in 1822 it was London's first public nude statue, and a fig leaf was added after complaints.

stops.name: Queen Elizabeth Gate & the Hyde Park Corner Screen
stops.note: Queen Elizabeth Gate was made for the Queen Mother's 90th birthday and unveiled by the Queen in 1993, with a red lion and a white unicorn in the middle; not everyone liked it, and critics called it a chocolate box. Next to it is the Screen, Decimus Burton's grand columned entrance to the park from 1825, with a frieze based on the Parthenon marbles.

stops.name: Apsley House & Wellington Arch
stops.note: Finish at 'Number 1, London': the first house you passed coming into town from the west.

title: Greenwich
meta: About 2½ hours · 3 km · start at Island Gardens DLR, or arrive by river boat
intro: Walk under the Thames through the 1902 foot tunnel, then the Cutty Sark, the Painted Hall, the Prime Meridian and one of the best views in London. Prefer to finish under the river? Do it in reverse and end at Island Gardens DLR.

stops.name: Island Gardens
stops.note: Start on the Isle of Dogs (Island Gardens DLR) for the view across the river to Greenwich that Canaletto painted. Then walk under the Thames.

stops.name: Greenwich Foot Tunnel
stops.note: Opened in 1902 so dockers could walk to work on the Isle of Dogs. You come up right beside the Cutty Sark. Under the Thames: Brunel's Thames Tunnel at Rotherhithe was the first ever dug under a river, and the Brunel Museum tells its story.

stops.name: Cutty Sark
stops.note: The world's last surviving tea clipper. You can walk underneath her hull.

stops.name: Old Royal Naval College & Painted Hall
stops.note: On the site of Greenwich Palace, where Henry VIII was born. The ceiling is called Britain's Sistine Chapel.

stops.name: Queen's House
stops.note: See the Tulip Stairs, the first self-supporting spiral staircase in Britain, and the scene of a famous 1966 ghost photo.

stops.name: National Maritime Museum
stops.note: Free. Nelson's coat from Trafalgar, with the bullet hole.

stops.name: Royal Observatory & Prime Meridian
stops.note: Stand with a foot in each hemisphere. The red time ball drops at exactly 1pm.

stops.name: General Wolfe statue viewpoint
stops.note: The Queen's House, the college, the river and the City behind. One of London's best views.

stops.name: Ranger's House
stops.note: The Bridgerton family home in the Netflix series. See it from outside.

stops.name: Greenwich Market
stops.note: Lunch, crafts and street food. Or head down to the Trafalgar Tavern on the river.

title: Harry Potter: West End & Westminster
intro: From the new Oxford Street flagship shop (opens 4 Nov 2026) to the Ministry of Magic phone box and the Knight Bus bridge.

stops.name: Harry Potter flagship, Oxford Street
stops.note: From 4 Nov 2026: a Diagon Alley street, a full-size Knight Bus and Butterbeer. Check opening before you go.

stops.name: Palace Theatre
stops.note: Home of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.

stops.name: House of MinaLima, Wardour Street
stops.note: Gallery of the designers who made the films' graphics: the Daily Prophet and the Marauder's Map. Check it's still here.

stops.name: Piccadilly Circus
stops.note: Harry, Ron and Hermione apparate here and dodge a bus in Deathly Hallows Part 1.

stops.name: Leicester Square
stops.note: The films' UK premieres were held here. Look for Harry on his broomstick.

stops.name: Scotland Place
stops.note: Where Harry and Mr Weasley use a red phone box to enter the Ministry of Magic.

stops.name: Westminster Underground station
stops.note: Harry and Mr Weasley go through the barriers on the way to his hearing.

stops.name: Lambeth Bridge
stops.note: The Knight Bus squeezes between two double-deckers. It's red to match the benches in the House of Lords.

title: Harry Potter: City & South Bank
intro: Gringotts, the wobbly bridge and two Leaky Cauldrons.

stops.name: Australia House, Strand
stops.note: Its grand hall was Gringotts bank. See it from outside.

stops.name: St Paul's & the Millennium Bridge
stops.note: The bridge the Death Eaters destroy. Londoners still call it the wobbly bridge.

stops.name: Borough Market, Stoney Street
stops.note: The Leaky Cauldron entrance in Prisoner of Azkaban. Good stop for lunch.

stops.name: Leadenhall Market
stops.note: The Leaky Cauldron's blue door in Philosopher's Stone, in Bull's Head Passage. On the site of the Roman forum.

title: Harry Potter: King's Cross
intro: Platform 9¾, the station that played King's Cross, and Grimmauld Place.

stops.name: Platform 9¾, King's Cross
stops.note: The scenes were filmed at platforms 4 and 5. There's no wall between 9 and 10 at all.

stops.name: St Pancras, Euston Road side
stops.note: The Gothic front you see in the films as 'King's Cross' is really St Pancras next door.

stops.name: Claremont Square
stops.note: The terrace used for the outside of 12 Grimmauld Place.

title: West End Music Trail
intro: Beatles, Bowie, Hendrix and punk, in a square mile of Mayfair and Soho. Finish with jazz at Ronnie Scott's.

stops.name: Handel & Hendrix House
stops.note: Two musicians, two hundred years apart, living next door to each other.

stops.name: 3 Savile Row
stops.note: The Apple rooftop, where the Beatles played their last public gig in January 1969.

stops.name: Heddon Street
stops.note: The Ziggy Stardust plaque, on the spot of the album cover photo.

stops.name: Carnaby Street
stops.note: Where the mods and the 60s bands bought their clothes.

stops.name: Berwick Street
stops.note: The Oasis cover street, and vinyl at Sister Ray.

stops.name: Marquee Club site, 90 Wardour Street
stops.note: The Who, Bowie and Hendrix all played here on their way up.

stops.name: St Anne's Court
stops.note: The David Bowie plaque at the old Trident Studios.

stops.name: The Toucan
stops.note: Where a young Jimi Hendrix jammed in the basement in 1966.

stops.name: Soho Square
stops.note: Kirsty MacColl's bench.

stops.name: Denmark Street
stops.note: Tin Pan Alley: the Stones' first studio and the Sex Pistols' old flat.

stops.name: The 100 Club
stops.note: Home of the 1976 Punk Special. Check what's on tonight.

title: LGBTQ+ Soho
intro: From the first Pride march in Trafalgar Square to the bars of Old Compton Street: a short walk through the history of gay London, with plenty of places to stop for a drink.

stops.name: Trafalgar Square
stops.note: On 1 July 1972 around 2,000 people gathered here for Britain's first Pride march, and walked to Hyde Park. Many were nervous of being seen; today Pride brings over a million people to these streets.

stops.name: Oscar Wilde memorial, Adelaide Street
stops.note: Maggi Hambling's 'A Conversation with Oscar Wilde' (1998): sit on the bench and chat with him. Wilde was jailed in 1895 for 'gross indecency'. The words carved on it are his: 'We are all in the gutter, but some of us are looking at the stars.'

stops.name: Heaven
stops.note: Under the arches of Charing Cross station since 1979, Heaven was one of the first big gay superclubs in Europe. Still home to Saturday's G-A-Y night.

stops.name: Ku Bar
stops.note: On the edge of Chinatown, one of London's biggest gay bars, over three floors.

stops.name: Rupert Street Bar
stops.note: Rupert Street has a cluster of gay bars, including this one and the Yard, hidden in a fairy-lit courtyard.

stops.name: Village Soho
stops.note: Often called Soho's first gay bar. Wardour Street and Old Compton Street became the heart of gay London in the 1980s and 90s, when bars started opening their windows to the street instead of hiding behind blacked-out glass.

stops.name: Admiral Duncan
stops.note: On 30 April 1999 a nail bomb exploded in this pub, killing three people and injuring dozens. Soho came out in force; the pub reopened weeks later. Look for the memorial inside.

stops.name: Comptons
stops.note: One of London's longest-running gay pubs, on the corner of Old Compton Street and Frith Street. Soho's village pub.

stops.name: She Soho
stops.note: London's best-known lesbian bar, down the stairs at the Charing Cross Road end of Old Compton Street.

stops.name: Soho Square
stops.note: Finish in the garden of Soho Square. On a Pride day this is party central; on any other day, a quiet place to sit with a coffee.

title: Ted Lasso's Richmond
intro: Believe! A short walk round the real Richmond behind AFC Richmond: the Crown & Anchor, Ted's street, the official shop and the river.

stops.name: Richmond station
stops.note: District line, Overground and trains from Waterloo. Or about 40 minutes by black cab from the West End.

stops.name: Richmond Theatre
stops.note: Where Rebecca hosts her charity gala.

stops.name: Richmond Green
stops.note: Where a little girl dribbles past Ted. A lovely green for a sit down.

stops.name: The Prince's Head
stops.note: The Crown & Anchor in the show. Sit on the bench outside for the photo.

stops.name: Paved Court (Ted's street)
stops.note: The little lane where Ted lives in the show.

stops.name: The Official Ted Lasso Store
stops.note: Kits, scarves and 'Believe' signs, a few doors from Ted's flat.

stops.name: Richmond Bridge
stops.note: The oldest surviving Thames bridge in London, and the riverside seen in the show.

stops.name: The White Cross
stops.note: Finish with a pint on the river, in the pub the Thames floods at high tide.

title: Whitehall Statues
intro: From Nelson down Whitehall, round the riverside memorials behind it and into Parliament Square: kings, generals, airmen and the women of the war, and the stories behind them. And a few minutes' walk from Trafalgar Square, in Waterloo Place, stands Banksy's 2026 flag statue.

stops.name: Nelson's Column, Trafalgar Square
stops.note: Nelson stands 52 metres up, looking down towards the fleet at Portsmouth. The four lions by Landseer were added in 1867. Look at the Fourth Plinth for the latest artwork.

stops.name: Charles I on horseback
stops.note: Cast in 1633 and the oldest bronze equestrian statue in London. Distances to London are measured from this spot. After the Civil War it was sold to a brazier to melt down – he hid it instead, and it came back after the Restoration. Charles looks down Whitehall to where he was executed.

stops.name: Horse Guards
stops.note: Two mounted troopers of the Household Cavalry stand guard here through the day. The Changing of the Guard is at 11am (10am on Sundays).

stops.name: Banqueting House
stops.note: The Rubens ceiling inside was paid for by Charles I – and on 30 January 1649 he stepped out of a window here onto the scaffold.

stops.name: The Gurkha statue
stops.note: Down Horse Guards Avenue: a Gurkha soldier, honouring the Nepalese soldiers who have served Britain for over 200 years.

stops.name: Chindit and RAF memorials
stops.note: On the Embankment: the Chindits, who fought behind Japanese lines in Burma, and the RAF memorial of 1923, its golden eagle facing out across the river.

stops.name: Battle of Britain Monument
stops.note: A long bronze frieze of pilots running to their planes and people in the Blitz, with the names of 'the Few' – the airmen of 1940 – along the sides.

stops.name: Women of World War II
stops.note: Back on Whitehall: no figures, just 17 sets of uniforms and work clothes hung up, as the women took them off at the end of the war.

stops.name: Monty, Slim and Alanbrooke
stops.note: Three Second World War commanders on the green outside the Ministry of Defence. Montgomery stands in his famous beret and duffel coat.

stops.name: The Cenotaph
stops.note: Lutyens' memorial to 'The Glorious Dead', made in stone in 1920. It looks straight, but its sides lean very slightly – if you carried the lines on up they would meet about 300 metres in the sky. Downing Street's gates are just opposite.

stops.name: Parliament Square statues
stops.note: Churchill faces Parliament, with Lincoln, Mandela, Gandhi and Millicent Fawcett – the first woman in the square, put up in 2018 – around the green.

stops.name: Boudicca, Westminster Bridge
stops.note: Finish with the warrior queen in her chariot, who burned Roman London to the ground. Big Ben is right behind you for the photo.

title: Changing the Guard: the two routes
intro: Two guards change on ceremony mornings. The foot guards (red route) march to Buckingham Palace from Wellington Barracks and St James's Palace. The mounted Household Cavalry (gold route) ride from Hyde Park Barracks, past the palace and down The Mall to Horse Guards, then back again. Usually Mon, Wed, Fri at 11:00 and Sunday at 10:00 (times run about an hour earlier on Sundays); it can be cancelled at short notice, so check householddivision.org.uk on the day. Best plan for a first-timer: Wellington Barracks at 10:15, The Mall by 10:40, then the Victoria Memorial or Horse Guards for 11:00.

stops.name: Wellington Barracks, Birdcage Walk
stops.note: 10:15 · The New Guard forms up for inspection and the band plays. Watch from the railings: far fewer people than at the palace. At 10:57 they march down Birdcage Walk to the palace. The Guards Museum is here too. Just round the corner are the Cockpit Steps, where two Coldstream Guards said they saw a headless woman in 1804.

stops.name: Friary Court, St James's Palace
stops.note: 10:25 · The Old Guard of the St James's Palace detachment is inspected, then marches down The Mall to the palace at 10:43, band leading.

stops.name: Hyde Park Barracks, Knightsbridge
stops.note: 10:28 · Home of the Household Cavalry. The new mounted guard rides out. The troopers are inspected first: the smartest gets the horse, the least smart does the longer duty on foot.

stops.name: Wellington Arch, Hyde Park Corner
stops.note: The riders come round the arch and onto Constitution Hill.

stops.name: Constitution Hill
stops.note: ~10:40 · A quieter spot to watch the cavalry ride by, with Green Park beside you. In 1840 a young man fired two shots at Queen Victoria's carriage here. Both missed, and she carried on calmly.

stops.name: The Mall (at Marlborough Road)
stops.note: 10:40–10:45 · Room to breathe. See the cavalry ride past and the Old Guard march by. When the mounted guard passes the foot guards they salute each other. Look up at the little ships on the lamp posts (Nelson's Fleet).

stops.name: Victoria Memorial
stops.note: The steps give the best view of the forecourt and both routes. Very busy: arrive well before 10:30.

stops.name: Buckingham Palace
stops.note: 11:00 · The Changing of the Guard on the forecourt, about 45 minutes. At 11:40 the Old Guard marches back to Wellington Barracks, and at 11:45 the new detachment marches up The Mall to St James's Palace.

stops.name: Horse Guards Parade
stops.note: 11:00 · The Changing of the King's Life Guard, about 30 minutes. Horse Guards is still the official entrance to both palaces. At 11:37 the old guard rides back up The Mall and Constitution Hill to Hyde Park Barracks.

title: Banksy: City & Shoreditch
intro: From a Banksy you can see in a museum to the ones still on London's walls, through the City and into Shoreditch. Banksy pieces can vanish overnight. Last checked 12 November 2026.

stops.name: London Museum, Smithfield
stops.note: Piranhas, the police box Banksy turned into a fish tank on Ludgate Hill in 2024, is on show free inside. The museum opens here on 28 November 2026.

stops.name: Barbican Basquiat pieces
stops.note: Two pieces from 2017 next to each other on the wall at Beech Street and Golden Lane, made for the Barbican's Basquiat exhibition: Basquiat's figure being stopped and searched by police, and a queue for a Ferris wheel made of his crowns. They're behind protective panels.

stops.name: art'otel London Hoxton
stops.note: Two 2004 Banksys rescued from the Foundry pub that used to stand here, now set into the hotel above its entrance on Rivington Street: a giant rat with a knife and fork, and a TV being thrown out of a window. Free to see from the street.

title: Banksy: West End
intro: Banksy from Marble Arch to St James's, ending with his newest piece in London. Banksy pieces can vanish overnight. Last checked 12 November 2026. Further afield: the elephants in Chelsea, the pelicans in Walthamstow, the rhino in Charlton and the Royal Family balcony on Stoke Newington Church Street. Check they're still there before you go.

stops.name: Moco Museum, Marble Arch
stops.note: Gallery pieces by Banksy alongside Warhol and Basquiat. Paid entry.

stops.name: Centre Point
stops.note: Two children lying on the pavement, one pointing up at the sky, stencilled at the foot of Centre Point in December 2025. Widely thought to be Banksy, though he only claimed its twin in Queen's Mews, Bayswater.

stops.name: Waterloo Place, St James's
stops.note: Banksy's flag statue, a suited man striding off his plinth with a flag over his face, which appeared in April 2026 beside Edward VII, Florence Nightingale and the Crimean War Memorial. Westminster Council has spent tens of thousands of pounds protecting it.
